claims.text: The proposed first-principles framework can separately compute phonon and electronic thermal-transport contributions in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed framework can explicitly incorporate the influence of minor oxygen impurities on transport.
The framework will improve quantitative predictive accuracy by roughly 30% over previous models.
The framework will accurately match independently measured lattice and electronic contributions at temperatures below 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K.
The bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy has an equiatomic composition.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen is representative of realistic processing conditions for HfNbTaTiZr.
Earlier simulations of this alloy typically represented a perfect, defect-free crystal.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
High-temperature conductivity measurements extending from 300 to 1200 K are available for an oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr specimen.
Alloy disorder and atomic-size differences produce local lattice distortions that can affect phonon transport.
Vibrational anharmonicity and oxygen-induced local distortions modulate phonon transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Electron scattering in HfNbTaTiZr is driven by alloy disorder and oxygen impurities.
Separating lattice and electronic transport avoids the oversimplification associated with use of a single Debye temperature.
Computing the lattice and electronic channels individually will improve prediction of total thermal conductivity in chemically complex, oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr.
The predicted total thermal conductivity will remain within ±30% of experiment over the examined temperature range.
Previous models conflated phonon and electronic contributions and consequently produced less accurate predictions.
The approach is expected to apply primarily from below 200 K through 1200 K and to samples containing about 1 wt.% oxygen.
Variations in impurity distribution and electron-phonon coupling strength create uncertainty in the magnitude of the predicted improvement.
Phonon-spectrum measurements and resistivity combined with the Wiedemann-Franz law can independently determine lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
Failure to predict the separate contributions with an overall error better than ±30%, or inconsistency with independently measured channel values, is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The claimed applicability ends at 1200 K, but the experiment extends to 1300 K and the rule can be read as requiring performance over that entire experimental range. Results between 1200 and 1300 K should not falsify a hypothesis explicitly bounded at 1200 K.

The hypothesis alternates between a 30% relative improvement over prior models and an absolute ±30% error threshold. These are different performance metrics, and the falsification rule does not specify the prior-model error needed to evaluate the claimed relative improvement.
